name: special-case
intent: Give the degenerate case of a type a value that honours the same interface with defined, benign behaviour, so callers never test for nil, zero, empty or 'unconfirmed' before using it and the type keeps its polymorphic contract.
problem: A query, lookup or factory sometimes cannot produce a real domain object - the row is missing, the customer is only an 'occupant', the amount is zero, the integration is switched off - and every caller then repeats the same null, zero or flag test in its own words. The duplicated checks drift apart, one forgotten branch becomes a runtime error or a silently wrong result, and the degenerate case itself has no name, no owner and no test.
context: Domain models, repositories and collaborators where a small set of degenerate cases is understood and has a domain-meaningful default behaviour: a lookup that may find nothing, a quantity or collection that may be empty, a record that is not yet confirmed, an integration that is disabled. It applies while the type is a value or collaborator reached through an interface - or through a closed set of variants in languages without inheritance - and the same default answer is right for most callers; it is the wrong tool when the failure itself has to stay diagnosable.
benefits: Call sites lose the nil/zero/'unknown' branches: the same code path serves the real and the degenerate value, so conditional logic moves out of every caller into one place beside the type.
The degenerate behaviour gets a name, an owner and a test, instead of being respelled - slightly differently - at each call site.
The case can carry domain meaning (an occupant customer, a zero discount policy, an empty payment history) where a bare null carries none.
New degenerate cases arrive as new implementations of the interface; existing callers stay untouched, which is the open/closed principle applied to absence.
It composes recursively: the special case returns further special cases (empty history, empty address, empty contract), so whole object graphs stay navigable without checks.
Stateless special cases are shareable singletons or flyweights: no per-call allocation, no lifecycle to manage and identity comparisons remain meaningful.
tradeoffs: A benign default can hide a real failure: a lost row, a failed lookup or a rejected authorisation becomes an object that answers zero, empty or 'unknown' instead of raising.
The interface gains a second implementation to keep in step; on a wide or volatile interface the special case is expensive to complete and easy to leave half-implemented.
The degenerate state is still a state: callers that must distinguish it have to ask (isUnknown, isEmpty); if they ask everywhere, the branching has been relocated rather than removed.
Callers may disagree on what the benign behaviour should be, so one special case turns into several - or into a configurable one whose configuration reintroduces the same branching.
The special case must never turn into a real object; if it can be filled in or replaced later, the design is a proxy and the invariant callers rely on is gone.
A stateful special case breaks the shared-instance property and buys a local simplification at the price of process-global state, lifetime and thread-safety questions.

participants.responsibility: Calls the interface as if a real object were present; contains no absence test and no knowledge of the degenerate state.
Declares the operations and postconditions every instance honours - interface, abstract class, protocol or closed set of variants - including the degenerate case.
Implementation for the found, confirmed or fully populated case; provides the ordinary behaviour.
Implementation with the same interface whose operations return the domain-defined benign result; immutable, usually stateless, and often the only instance of its class.
The one place that knows the value is degenerate: converts a miss, a zero quantity or an unconfirmed record into the special case and returns it as the abstract type.
Optional variant that keeps the partial information available where the real object could not be produced (the requested id, the unknown name) and answers the interface from it.

use_cases: Repository lookups that may miss: an unknown customer ('occupant'), a missing product or account whose reads should still answer.
Zero and empty quantities: a zero discount policy, an empty order history, an empty basket that still supports every operation.
Provisional records: unconfirmed, partially migrated or not-yet-verified data that must be readable before it is complete.
Switched-off collaborations: a no-op logger, metrics sink, cache or event collector that keeps injection sites branch-free.
Recursive structures: the empty leaf or empty list node of a tree, so traversals need no special case at every level.
Presentation and reporting: an unrecognised or absent state that must still render something meaningful instead of a blank field.

Standard-library empty collections: Java's Collections.emptyList()/List.of() and .NET's Enumerable.Empty<T>() are shared immutable zero-element collections returned instead of null, so callers iterate and query size with no guard.

Branch-free collaborators in client libraries: Go's net/http.NoBody (Read returns EOF, Close a no-op, introduced in Go 1.8 to replace the fragile nil-body convention for zero-byte request bodies) and .NET's Task.CompletedTask let code with nothing to send or await still honour the interface.
avoid_when: Callers must know why there is no value (not found vs. not authorised vs. upstream failure): use Option/Result/Either or an exception that carries the reason.
The case is exceptional and rare: an explicit exception is louder, cheaper and easier to observe than a parallel implementation.
The interface is large or volatile, or the degenerate behaviour is not domain-meaningful: one guarded null check in the factory is simpler and more honest.
Different callers need different defaults for the same type: pass an explicit policy or strategy instead of overloading one special case.
The type has no sane benign behaviour at all (no meaningful zero, empty or unknown semantics): there is nothing to implement, so model the absence explicitly instead.
anti_patterns: Null object everywhere: replacing a genuine failure with a do-nothing implementation so errors become silent no-ops.
Flag carrier: a special case with mutable fields or isX() flags that callers immediately test, which relocates the null check instead of removing it.
Transformable special case: an object that starts benign and later becomes real - a proxy with different invariants wearing the pattern's name.
Class explosion: one special case per caller expectation (plus a second one per nested type) instead of one per domain case.
Lying defaults: an unknown object that reports plausible business values (balance 0, plan basic) so the UI presents invented data as fact.
design_principles: Tell, don't ask: callers invoke behaviour instead of inspecting the value's state.
Polymorphism over type tests: the degenerate case is a subtype, not a branch.
Single responsibility: the definition of the default behaviour lives once, with the type it belongs to.
Open/closed: a new degenerate case is a new implementation, not an edit to every caller.
Liskov substitution: the special case must honour the interface's postconditions and must not throw, or callers cannot treat it uniformly.
Encapsulation: callers do not need to know why the value is degenerate.
best_practices: Name the case after its domain meaning (UnknownCustomer, Occupant, ZeroDiscount, NoMetrics), never after the mechanism (NullCustomer).
Keep special cases immutable and, when they are stateless, share exactly one instance.
Decide at the boundary: the factory, repository or mapper turns absence into the special case, so no other code sees raw nil, zero or sentinel values.
Write the benign behaviour down operation by operation, and run the same contract tests against the real implementation and the special case.
Expose one explicit predicate (isUnknown) for callers that genuinely must distinguish the case, and treat widespread use of it as a design smell.
Never let the special case throw and never let it mutate into a real object; when the caller must decide, return an explicit Option/Result instead.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002), Base Patterns - Special Case: a subclass that provides special behaviour for particular cases (nulls, infinity, the utility customer known only as 'occupant'); instead of returning null or an odd value, return a special case with the same interface the caller expects.

Woolf, Null Object, in Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 (1997) - the absence-only relative: a surrogate with the same interface that does nothing; consequences include needing a NullObject per abstraction, clients disagreeing on what 'do nothing' means, and the rule that a null object never transforms into a real one (that would be a Proxy).

https://mail.python.org/pipermail/python-ideas/2015-September/036322.html - python-ideas critique of a built-in Null object: chaining a benign null value spreads 'null infection', contaminating data and hiding the real error instead of surfacing it.
